scenes.heading: Same ratio, different substances
scenes.body: An empirical formula gives composition. It does not identify the substance.
scenes.callout: First find the ratio of atoms.
scenes.caption: Different substances can share an empirical formula.

voiceover.text: We already know how to turn grams into moles. Now we can use that idea to work backwards from a compound's composition. Glucose and formaldehyde are very different substances. Yet both have the same simplest ratio of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms: one to two to one. So a composition result can give us a useful clue without telling us exactly what the substance is. The first clue is an empirical formula. Let's see how a measurement of mass becomes a ratio of atoms.

scenes.heading: Ratio versus actual count
scenes.body: Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio. Molecular formula: atoms in one molecule.

bullets.text: Glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆. Count ratio 6:12:6.
Formaldehyde: CH₂O. Count ratio 1:2:1.

scenes.secondary: Counting model only. Blocks do not show bonds or separate glucose fragments.

voiceover.text: Glucose has six carbon atoms, twelve hydrogens and six oxygens in each molecule. That six to twelve to six ratio reduces to one to two to one, written C H two O. Formaldehyde already has one carbon, two hydrogens and one oxygen. Its formula reduces to the same ratio. The empirical formula keeps the proportion. The molecular formula keeps the actual atom count in one molecule. These blocks are a counting model; they don't show how the atoms are bonded.

scenes.heading: Mass percentage
scenes.callout: Atom ratios and mass percentages describe different relationships.
scenes.caption: Mass percentage compares an element’s mass contribution with the total.

bullets.text: Mass percentage = element mass ÷ total mass × 100.

voiceover.text: Percentage composition measures a different relationship: how much of a compound's mass comes from each element. For C H two O, the carbon contributes twelve point zero one out of a total of thirty point zero two six grams per mole, using our supplied values. Divide the carbon contribution by the total, then multiply by one hundred. That's about forty percent carbon by mass. The hydrogen count is twice the carbon count, but hydrogen atoms are much lighter. Atom ratios and mass percentages won't generally be the same numbers.

voiceover.text: Balancing is an atom-accounting check. The same atoms have to appear on both sides, because an ordinary chemical reaction rearranges them. We adjust the numbers of whole entities, keeping each formula intact. That's why the coefficients can give us an amount ratio. The subscripts help us check the atom totals, but they aren't the numbers we use for the wanted-over-known conversion.

voiceover.text: There are two easy ways to get a plausible-looking wrong answer. One is taking the little numbers inside the formulas as the mole ratio. The other is using the right coefficients upside down. A quick sense-check helps. If the reaction needs twice as much acid as base, an acid answer that's half the base amount doesn't fit the equation. For a product prediction, we also need the stated reactant amount to react completely, with enough of the other reactants. The equation alone can't guarantee what we'll recover in the lab.

voiceover.text: Burn twelve grams of carbon and you can make about forty-four grams of carbon dioxide. That sounds like a very generous reaction. Where did the extra mass come from? voiceover.text: Mass-to-mass stoichiometry. Connecting the reaction's amounts to grams.

scenes.caption: A 1:1 mole ratio does not imply equal masses.

voiceover.text: From the last lesson, a balanced equation compares mole amounts. Here carbon and carbon dioxide are one for one in moles. But one mole of carbon dioxide includes oxygen, so it weighs more than one mole of carbon. That's why the one-to-one coefficients aren't a one-to-one mass ratio. Carbon's molar mass connects its grams to its moles. The equation then connects those moles to carbon dioxide moles. Carbon dioxide's own molar mass takes us back to grams. The moving packet marks a calculation step. These equal piles show the one-to-one amount relationship, not literal particles travelling across a bridge.

scenes.caption: Predicted product mass depends on stated reaction and sample conditions.

voiceover.text: There is a condition hiding behind a product prediction: the stated reactant amount has to react completely by the equation we're using. For the carbon example, that means enough oxygen and complete combustion to carbon dioxide. For the iron example, we'll start with pure iron three oxide, rather than assuming a whole ore sample is pure oxide. The answer is a theoretical mass under those conditions. What we actually collect can be lower because the reaction or recovery isn't perfect. We'll deal with limiting supplies and measured yield in their own lessons.

voiceover.text: If mass-to-mole conversion and mole ratios already make sense, this is where they meet. We divide the known mass by that substance's molar mass. The units become moles. We then multiply by the wanted coefficient over the known coefficient, because the equation compares amounts. Finally, the wanted substance's molar mass turns its moles into grams. Each end needs the molar mass of the substance at that end. The two numbers might happen to be equal; their identity still matters. You can combine the three relationships into one expression. Showing the mole pathway helps us see why that expression works.

voiceover.text: Let's put numbers on the carbon question. Twelve point zero grams of pure carbon burns completely, with enough oxygen. What carbon dioxide mass does the equation predict? Carbon's molar mass turns the given mass into an amount: just under one mole. That's an approximation for talking about the result; the calculation keeps the unrounded value. The equation gives one mole of carbon dioxide for each mole of carbon, so the product amount is the same. For the mass, we need carbon dioxide's own molar mass. It includes one carbon and two oxygens, not just the carbon we started with. Multiplying by that molar mass gives forty-four point zero grams, to three significant figures. About thirty-two grams came from oxygen. Counting both starting substances, mass is conserved.

scenes.heading: Another hundred buns?
scenes.body: 5 buns. 4 patties. One of each per burger.
scenes.callout: 4 burgers. The patties set the limit.
scenes.caption: 5 buns + 4 patties. One of each per burger. How many complete burgers?

voiceover.text: You're making burgers. Five buns, four patties. That's four burgers, right? One lonely bun left over. Buying another hundred buns won't help. You've still got no patties. Chemistry has exactly this problem, except the recipe can ask for two of one ingredient. And that's where the obvious answer can be wrong. The ingredient that runs out sets the limit. In chemistry, that's the limiting reagent. The balanced equation tells us the recipe.

scenes.caption: Limiting Reagents and Theoretical Yield (Year 11 Chemistry, Module 2, Lesson 13)

voiceover.text: Limiting reagents. What runs out, what gets made, and what's left.

scenes.heading: No oxygen, no more water
scenes.body: The limiting reagent is consumed completely. The excess reagent has some left over.

bullets.text: 2 H₂ + 1 O₂ makes 2 H₂O.
Start: 10 H₂ and 4 O₂ molecules.
End: 8 H₂O and 2 H₂ molecules remain.

scenes.secondary: Schematic counts, not molecular collisions or a rate experiment.
scenes.callout: Oxygen runs out. More hydrogen cannot make more water.
scenes.caption: Limiting runs out first and sets the yield; excess is left over.

voiceover.text: Here's the same idea with hydrogen and oxygen. The recipe needs two hydrogen molecules for every oxygen molecule, making two water molecules. We've got ten hydrogen and four oxygen. Enough for four batches. There goes the oxygen. We've made eight water molecules, with two hydrogen molecules still sitting there. They've got nobody left to react with. More hydrogen won't get us any more water. Oxygen is limiting; hydrogen is in excess. This is a counting model, so those neat batches aren't real collisions, and the graph isn't showing reaction speed.

scenes.heading: The smaller pile wins?
scenes.body: The starting amounts suggest one answer. Does the recipe agree?

bullets.text: Na: 0.435 mol; Cl₂: 0.282 mol.
Divide by coefficients: 2 for Na, 1 for Cl₂.
Compare: 0.218 < 0.282. Sodium is limiting.

scenes.secondary: Each value measures equation-sized reaction capacity.
scenes.callout: The recipe decides what runs out.
scenes.caption: Moles ÷ coefficient for each reactant; smallest is limiting.

voiceover.text: Now here's the trap. We've got about zero point four three five moles of sodium, and zero point two eight two moles of chlorine gas. Less chlorine. So chlorine runs out first? Sounds reasonable. But the equation needs twice as much sodium: two sodium for one chlorine. Sodium's bigger supply has a bigger job to do. Dividing by two gives sodium about zero point two one eight batches' worth. Chlorine gives zero point two eight two, because its coefficient is one. Sodium runs out first. The recipe decided it. These are mole amounts per equation coefficient, not literal little batches in a beaker.

voiceover.text: That surprising result is the key to this calculation. Ten point zero grams of sodium and twenty point zero grams of chlorine gas. How much sodium chloride could we make, and how much chlorine would be left? Grams alone can't tell us who runs out, because the particles have different masses. Using the supplied molar masses, we get about zero point four three five moles of sodium and zero point two eight two moles of chlorine. Same comparison we just saw: sodium is limiting. Now the nice part. The equation has two sodium and two sodium chloride, so their mole ratio is one to one. That sodium amount gives a theoretical yield of twenty-five point four grams of sodium chloride. The chlorine hasn't all disappeared, though. The recipe uses one chlorine for two sodium, so only about zero point two one seven five moles of chlorine react. What's left is the starting amount minus that amount: four point five eight grams of chlorine. The working keeps extra digits; these final masses are rounded to three significant figures.

scenes.secondary: Divide by coefficients. Sodium supports fewer reaction batches.

voiceover.text: It's tempting to look for the smallest number and call it a day. Our chlorine example would catch you out. There were fewer moles of chlorine, but sodium was required in a two-to-one ratio. That's why the coefficients matter. And theoretical yield is a ceiling for the stated reaction, not a promise about what we'll collect in the lab. We're assuming the limiting reagent is completely consumed in the stated reaction. Actual yield can be lower.

scenes.heading: The recipe wins
points: Reaction capacity: moles divided by the equation coefficient.
Theoretical yield: set by the reactant that runs out.
Excess left: starting amount minus amount reacted.
scenes.caption: The recipe decides what runs out, the yield and the leftovers.

voiceover.text: So the useful question isn't, 'Which pile looks smaller?' It's, 'How much reaction can each supply support?' Moles account for particle numbers; the coefficients account for the recipe. Whichever runs out sets the theoretical yield. The excess is whatever we started with minus whatever reacted. Once those ideas click, the calculation has a reason behind it. And the leftover bun finally makes sense.
